analysis.one_liner: Lets employers exclude voluntary off-hours training from paid work time.
analysis.headline: The bill would have let employers stop paying hourly workers for voluntary off-hours training time; it drew a sponsor plus 8 Republican cosponsors but died in committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the Fair Labor Standards Act, time an hourly employee spends working generally must be paid, including overtime. This bill would write into the law that employers do not have to pay for training, lectures, or similar activities held outside regular work hours, even when the employer offers or runs the training, as long as attendance is voluntary, staying away does not hurt the worker's job conditions, and the worker does no productive work during it. It would also lock in an existing exclusion for clothes-changing and washing time covered by union contracts.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers of hourly workers — especially in retail, food service, hospitality, and warehousing, where off-hours training is common — would save on wages and overtime. The bill's stated framing is worker flexibility, but its legal effect is to reduce compensable time; a worker who attends employer-offered training outside regular hours would do it unpaid.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would add training and lecture time to the Fair Labor Standards Act's list of excluded activities, so employers would owe no wages or overtime for that time even when they offer the training themselves, provided it is outside regular hours, voluntary, and free of productive work.

By writing the exclusion into the statute itself, the bill would take the pay question out of the Labor Department's hands and drop the current regulation's requirement that unpaid training not be directly related to the employee's job, meaning job-specific training could go unpaid.

analysis.who_pays: Hourly workers who spend their own off-hours time in employer-provided training would bear the cost: that time would no longer be paid or count toward overtime. The savings come out of workers' paychecks and flow to their employers.

drawbacks.text: Workers would not be paid for employer-offered training that builds skills the employer relies on, shifting the cost of developing the workforce onto the workers themselves.

The bill's only real protection against unpaid work is the word 'voluntary' plus a ban on retaliation-like effects — attendance is unpaid even when the training is specific to the job, a condition current Labor Department rules include — and subtle pressure to attend would be hard to police.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For employers this is a straightforward cost cut: fewer paid hours and less overtime liability. For hourly workers it is a pay cut for any off-hours training they attend, and the safeguards — voluntariness, no adverse conditions, no productive work — narrow but do not eliminate the loss, because job-specific training the employer benefits from would go unpaid. On balance the bill transfers money from low-wage workers to their employers rather than creating new education opportunity.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Education and Labor Committee, which never took it up before the two-year Congress ended, so it died without a hearing, a vote, or a companion in the Senate.

narrative.text: Representative Ashley Hinson introduced the bill on April 1, 2022, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor.
Eight House Republicans signed on as cosponsors; no Democrat did.
The committee took no further action — no markup, no hearing on the bill, no vote — and the bill expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained anything concrete, because the bill never became law. Hourly workers came out ahead relative to the bill's passage: they kept existing pay rules under which required or job-related training time is compensable.

for.name: Rep. Ashley Hinson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, which would exclude voluntary off-hours training from paid hours worked under the Fair Labor Standards Act.

for.name: 8 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all of the bill's supporters were Republicans.

against.name: Rep. Bobby Scott
against.role: Chair, House Education and Labor Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for consideration; it received no markup, hearing, or vote after referral and died at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 9 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans and no Democrat joined, and the Democratic chair of the committee to which it was referred never acted on it; no vote was ever taken, so the partisan split is inferred from sponsorship rather than a roll call.

industries.industry: Employers of hourly workers (retail, food service, hospitality, warehousing)
industries.note: The bill would let these employers stop paying wages and overtime for off-hours training time, even training they themselves offer and run, cutting labor costs at the direct expense of workers' paychecks. The savings are largest for businesses that require or encourage employees to complete training outside scheduled shifts.
